plates.reference: Own code graphic: on period paper, an inked receptor-affinity and half-life curve from Snyder, Katims, Annau, Bruns & Daly (May 1981, PNAS) shows caffeine competitively blocking brain adenosine receptors at 10–50 micromolar blood concentrations (1–2 cups of coffee) vs >1,000 micromolar needed for phosphodiesterase inhibition, alongside the ~5-hour human metabolic half-life curve showing unblocked adenosine accumulation causing the afternoon crash.

teach_overlay.detail: Inked receptor-affinity & half-life curve on period paper from Snyder, Katims, Annau, Bruns & Daly (May 1981, PNAS) showing caffeine competitively blocking brain adenosine receptors at 10–50 micromolar blood concentrations (1–2 cups of coffee) vs >1,000 micromolar needed for phosphodiesterase inhibition, alongside the ~5-hour human metabolic half-life curve showing unblocked adenosine accumulation causing the afternoon crash
teach_overlay.scale: a single cup of coffee floods your bloodstream with roughly three hundred quintillion caffeine molecules — parking a fake key inside up to half of your brain's sleep receptors within forty-five minutes
